grammar.name: Inversion after negative adverbials
grammar.rule: Some negative words can start a sentence: Seldom, Rarely, Never, No sooner...than, Little did..., Under no circumstances. When one of these words comes first, you swap the subject and the auxiliary verb, just like in a question.
grammar.formula: Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + main verb
grammar.example: Seldom have researchers observed such a rapid shift in the future of work and automation.
grammar.tip: Only swap the word order when the negative word is at the very start of the sentence. If it stays in its usual place in the middle, do not change the order.

grammar.name: Inversion in formal conditionals
grammar.rule: In formal writing, you can leave out the word 'if' in some conditional sentences. Instead, you start the clause with Had, Were or Should, and swap the subject and the verb.
grammar.formula: Had/Were/Should + subject + (not) + past participle / base form, ...
grammar.example: Had it not been for sustained investment, progress on the future of work and automation would have stalled entirely.
grammar.tip: Use this pattern only in formal writing. Never use 'if' and the inverted word order together in the same sentence.

grammar.name: It-cleft sentences
grammar.rule: An it-cleft sentence puts special focus on one part of a sentence — often the real cause, person, or reason.
grammar.formula: It + is/was + emphasised element + that/who + remainder of clause
grammar.example: It is precisely the lack of coordinated policy that undermines progress on the future of work and automation.
grammar.tip: Make sure 'is' or 'was' matches the tense of the rest of the text. Do not use more than one it-cleft in the same paragraph.

grammar.name: Mixed conditional (past cause, present result)
grammar.rule: This links an unreal condition in the past to its unreal result now, in the present. It connects two different time periods in one sentence.
grammar.formula: If + past perfect, ... would + base verb
grammar.example: If policymakers had acted sooner on the future of work and automation, the situation would not be so urgent today.
grammar.tip: Before you write, keep the two time periods clear in your mind: the condition is in the past, and the result is in the present.

grammar.name: Mixed conditional (present cause, past result)
grammar.rule: This links an unreal situation now with an unreal result in the past. It is less common, but useful when you need to be precise.
grammar.formula: If + past simple, ... would have + past participle
grammar.example: If the public were less resistant to change, the reforms on the future of work and automation would have passed years ago.
grammar.tip: Use this pattern only occasionally, and only when it is really clear that a present situation affected a past result.

grammar.name: Participle clauses of reason (present participle)
grammar.rule: This is a shorter way to give a reason. You use an -ing verb instead of 'because' or 'since'.
grammar.example: Recognising the risks associated with exam mindset, wellbeing and peak performance, several governments have introduced new safeguards.
grammar.tip: The person or thing doing the -ing action must be the same as the subject of the main sentence. Otherwise, the meaning becomes unclear.

grammar.name: Perfect participle clauses (sequence)

grammar.tip: Use 'having + past participle' (not just '-ing') whenever the order of events is important.

grammar.tip: This is different from a simple passive sentence. The causative shows that the subject arranged the action — not just that it happened to them.

grammar.name: Mandative subjunctive
grammar.rule: This is used after words like recommend, insist, essential, or vital — words that show a recommendation, a demand, or a necessity.
grammar.formula: Subject + suggest/recommend/insist + that + subject + base verb (no -s, no tense change)
grammar.example: Experts recommend that policy on exam mindset, wellbeing and peak performance be reviewed on an annual basis.
grammar.tip: The verb after 'that' always stays in its base form. It never changes for person or tense: use 'be reviewed', not 'is reviewed' or 'was reviewed'.
